name: David Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an underground loader at a gold mine, the kind we call a bogger, which scoops broken rock from the stopes and carries it to the ore pass. I'm leading hand on my shift, so I sort out who goes to which level and I do the shift report at the end. Most of the day I'm in the cab, nine hundred metres down, with headlights and a radio. The mine's owned by a smaller company and the pay is behind the big operators, which is why I've only got a few hundred dollars saved.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's skilled. Getting a full bucket in a tight drive without touching the walls takes years. What wears me out is the heat down there and the four-hour round trip on days off to see my mum. Priya, my girlfriend, is a nurse at the hospital in town, and with her shifts and mine we sometimes don't see each other for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's pretty much what I already see. The AI stuff helps with paperwork and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so to the lads who thought robots were taking over next year. At work I'd say let's focus on the things that matter, like heat stress and the pay gap with the bigger mines. Online I'd just share the union's wage comparison again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine on the job but still stuck on money. I'm already the best bogger operator on the shift and I still earn less than a junior at the big mine two hours away. AI being hype doesn't make the company any less tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and use the AI thing on my phone for the shift report now and then, it saves me twenty minutes. I'd push the union delegate to start bargaining early. And I'd put fifty dollars a week aside, which is about all I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. A bit stuck. It's not scary, it's just slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the big mine two hours away. Would you move for better pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it a lot. But Priya's job is here and she loves the hospital. So right now I stay and fight for better pay where I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If one bill came in that you couldn't pay, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the car rego, the registration, because it all comes at once. Last year I put it on a credit card and I'm still paying that off. That's the kind of thing that keeps me up, not robots.

say: I'd tell the lads the **robot panic** was overblown.
Work talk should focus on **heat stress** and the pay gap with bigger mines.
think: My **job is fine**, but my money is still stuck.
I'm the best on shift yet earn less than a **junior** at the big mine.
do: Use the phone **AI app** now and then to write shift reports.
Push the **union delegate** to start bargaining early.
feel: **Okay** but stuck, because the problem is slow pay, not fear.
S0.quote: I'm already the best bogger operator on the shift and I still earn less than a junior at the big mine two hours away.
fieldNote: His worries are **pay and bills**, not technology, in this world.
He stays put because of **Priya's job**, which gives the household a steadier second income.
He uses AI in a **small, practical** way for reports.

steps.text: Use the phone AI app to write the end-of-shift report
Ask the union delegate to start pay bargaining early
Put fifty dollars a week into a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots spreading slowly. We already have tele-remote boggers on the level below, run from a room on the surface.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is fine if workers share in it. At the union I'd say we need a deal on remote operation before it spreads, so current operators get first go. Online I'd say this is why we need unions more, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the remote room is where the jobs go. One operator up top can run two or three loaders. So the mine needs fewer of us, and I want to be one of the ones they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for the tele-remote course as soon as it opens, it's six weeks. I'd ask the AI on my phone to help me study the manuals. I'd get the union to ask for every operator to be offered the same training, not just the favourites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but okay, because I can see a path. I'd feel worse for the older guys who don't want to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe, who's fifty-eight and has been down there thirty years. He can feel the rock through the bucket, but he won't touch a joystick in an air-conditioned room. I'd try to get him a role training the young ones, while there still are young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the remote job pay more or less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the same at first, but without the underground allowance, so less in my pocket. That's the bit nobody says out loud. I'd need the union to fight for that allowance to stay.

say: Change is fine if **workers share** in it.
We need a **union deal** on remote operation so current operators get first go.
think: The **remote room** is where the jobs go, with one operator running several loaders.
The mine will need **fewer of us**, and I want to be kept.
do: **Sign up** for the six-week tele-remote course when it opens.
Use the phone **AI app** to help study the loader manuals.
Get the union to demand **equal training** for every operator.
feel: **Nervous** but okay, because he can see a path.
**Worried** for older operators who won't learn remote work.
S1.quote: One operator up top can run two or three loaders. So the mine needs fewer of us, and I want to be one of the ones they keep.
fieldNote: He already sees **tele-remote** loaders, so this world feels close.
He worries about losing the **underground allowance**, a hidden pay cut.
His concern for **Joe** shows a team lead's sense of duty.

steps.text: Enrol in the six-week tele-remote loader course
Study the loader manuals with the phone AI app
Get the union to secure equal training and keep the allowance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028 for the thinking work and 2031 for robots. The remote room is thinking work, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say government needs to tax the companies that profit and pay people while they retrain. At work I'd say we stick together and we don't let them pick us off one by one. Online I'd probably get into arguments, I'm not good at staying out of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the tele-remote plan from before falls apart. If AI can do any thinking work by 2028, it can run the loaders from the surface control room, and then the robots come for the hands-on bits by 2031. So I've got maybe three years down there and maybe none up top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop banking on the remote course and look for something that needs hands longer, like becoming a diesel fitter. I'd ask Priya if we could live on her pay for a while if I took an apprentice wage. I'd go to every union meeting and push for a redundancy deal with retraining money in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. Two years is nothing. Priya would be steadier about it than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask Priya to carry you for a while. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it at the kitchen table with the budget printed out. I'd say it's three years, not forever, and I'd come out a fitter. She'd say yes, but I'd hate asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fitters work on machines that might be robots by 2031. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. But someone has to fix the robots for a while, and that's hands and tools in the dirt. It's the best bet I can see, not a safe one.

say: Government should **tax** the companies that profit and fund retraining.
Workers must **stick together** so the company can't pick us off.
think: The **remote-room** plan fails, because AI can run it from 2028.
I'd have roughly **three years** underground before robots arrive in 2031.
do: Switch from the remote course to a **diesel fitter** apprenticeship.
**Ask Priya** to carry the household on her nurse's pay for a while.
Push at union meetings for a **redundancy deal** with retraining money.
feel: **Frightened**, because two years of warning is almost nothing.
S2.quote: If AI can do any thinking work by 2028, it can run the loaders from the surface control room, and then the robots come for the hands-on bits by 2031.
fieldNote: He quickly sees that **thinking AI** removes the remote-room escape route.
Leaning on **Priya's income** is his safety net and a source of discomfort.
He chooses fitting as the **best bet**, not a safe one.

steps.text: Apply for a diesel fitter apprenticeship at the mine
Live on Priya's nurse pay during the apprentice years
Push the union for a redundancy deal with retraining money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's long enough to do something but short enough that I can't muck around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them. At work I'd push for the company to pay for apprenticeships for current operators. Online I'd share whatever the union puts out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is roughly one fitter apprenticeship plus a bit. If I start in the next year, I finish before AGI and have a trade before the robots come in 2034. That feels like a real plan rather than a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the diesel fitter apprenticeship within the year, maybe through the mine's own program. I'd keep a few shifts on the bogger to keep some income. And I'd build up savings for a year before I start, so we're not leaning on Priya from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a knot in my stomach. It's doable, but it's a lot of years on low pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you need saved before starting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like two months of rent, about four thousand dollars. On my pay that's a year of being careful, no trips to the coast. It's tight but I could do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use the AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, for study mostly, like asking it to explain a hydraulic diagram. I don't trust it to do my job, but it's a decent tutor. Everyone on the course will be using it.

The company should **pay for apprenticeships** for current operators.
think: Five years fits one **fitter apprenticeship**, finished before AGI in 2031.
Starting soon feels like a **real plan** rather than a scramble.
do: Start a **diesel fitter apprenticeship** within the year.
Keep **a few shifts** on the loader to hold some income.
**Save** about four thousand dollars before starting.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a knot about years of low apprentice pay.
S3.quote: Five years is roughly one fitter apprenticeship plus a bit.
fieldNote: Five years turns panic into a **timed plan**.
He wants a **savings buffer** first so he doesn't lean on Priya at once.
He uses AI as a **study tutor**, not as a work tool.

steps.text: Start the mine's diesel fitter apprenticeship within the year
Save four thousand dollars, about two months' rent, before starting
Ask a study AI to explain hydraulic diagrams

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, and thirteen until robots do the loader work. That's a long way off for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse to leave anyone behind with that much time. At the union I'd say we should be planning the next three pay deals around retraining. Online I'd be calmer than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably stay on the loader for a good while. I'd still get a trade, but without rushing it. My bigger worry would be money, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep operating for the next two or three years and save. Then I'd start an apprenticeship around thirty. I'd also take on more of the union delegate role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. There's time to breathe, but the pay problem is still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until thirty instead of starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Priya and I want to get a deposit together first. If I go on apprentice pay now, that never happens. With ten years I can do it in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone just starting underground in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the machine, and then learn how to fix it. Operators come and go, but the person who knows why it broke is the last one out. That's what I'd tell my younger cousin, anyway.

say: With ten years there's **no excuse** to leave anyone behind.
The next **three pay deals** should be built around retraining.
think: I'd stay on the **loader** for a good while yet.
My bigger worry would still be **money**, not robots.
do: Keep operating and **save** for two or three years.
Take on more of the **union delegate** role.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with time to breathe but the pay problem unsolved.
S4.quote: Operators come and go, but the person who knows why it broke is the last one out.
fieldNote: A decade lets him put the **house deposit** before retraining.
His **pay problem** stays the same in every picture.
He moves towards **union leadership** as the timeline lengthens.

steps.text: Save with Priya towards a house deposit for two or three years
Start a fitter apprenticeship around age thirty
Stand for the union delegate role on his shift

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. The remote job I was counting on would vanish with the thinking AI, and I'd have three years before the robots. What would help is the company paying for apprenticeships for its own operators, and a government payment that lets you train without your partner carrying you.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the heat. People think robots are only about saving money, but nine hundred metres down at thirty-five degrees, a robot doing the worst stopes would save lives. I just want the people who did that work to still have a living.

headlineQuote: Nine hundred metres down at thirty-five degrees, a robot doing the worst stopes would save lives. I just want the people who did that work to still have a living.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old** underground loader operator and leading hand at a gold mine.
He earns below the big mines, has **a few hundred** dollars saved, and lives with Priya, a nurse.
He is **pro-union** and uses AI now and then for reports and study.
In slow pictures he plans **tele-remote** training; in fast ones he switches to a fitter apprenticeship.
He is **alarmed** in AGI by 2028 but sees a clear plan with five or ten years.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, because thinking AI wipes out the remote-room job he counted on.
whatWouldHelp: The company paying for **apprenticeships** for its own operators.
A **government payment** during retraining so his partner doesn't have to carry him.
